beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Access is not absorption
beats.got: nothing new, the lecture title

beats.trigger: Access is a switch somebody flips, and it completes in a minute.
beats.got: license count and real use are different numbers. I know that, but it's said well.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: a good agent-built proposal died because leadership hadn't done the work themselves. A good output doesn't mean the org acts on it.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: you can copy context, boundary and checks but not the person who answers for the agent. That's the maintenance question I haven't answered.

take_homes: Stop asking how to share my agent and ask what job the teammate is doing today and what they use for it. Then pick context, skill, output or interface from that answer.
Every plan needs a named owner on the people side. My setups usually have a polished technical half and nobody to maintain them.
Access isn't adoption. The sales setup I'd build over a weekend could end up as another Confluence-AI-style thing nobody opens.

monday.move: Talk to our head of sales about how she preps for customer calls today. I won't build anything before that.
monday.who: Head of sales, plus one SDR if she agrees
monday.when: Monday or Tuesday, 20 minutes, before I touch any setup
monday.stop_condition: If she doesn't have a repeated job the agent could take, or won't own it afterwards, I park the sales idea.
monday.blocker: I want to start building the weekend project, and nobody has asked for it or agreed to maintain it.

misconception.why: The story is about a good, plausible agent output that still went nowhere. So good output doesn't mean the outcome is good. I still think checking is for beginners, because the module never made me check an output, and I skipped the spot-check lines. What shook me is that I haven't tested whether anyone wants what I build.

one_line: it's mostly not about the tech. The useful part is the question about what makes someone drop their current way of working, and the pace was fine for me except the repeated bits.
